newsitem.title: USA: Spy Factory, owner plead guilty to smuggling.
newsitem.headline: Spy Factory, owner plead guilty to smuggling.

text.p: Federal authorities shut down the Spy Factory, the nation's largest chain of "spy shops," on Monday after the company and its owner pleaded guilty to smuggling and selling illegal bugging and wiretapping devices.

The San Antonio, Texas-based chain was closed shortly after a plea hearing in Manhattan federal court at which U.S. District Judge Sonia Sotomayor ordered Spy Factory and all of its assets forfeited to the United States.

Mary Jo White, U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York, told a news conference that Customs Service agents closed Spy Factory's headquarters and were in the process of padlocking its 11 stores. She said the investigation was continuing.
Spy Factory pleaded guilty to 69 counts of money laundering, smuggling, selling illegal wiretapping and bugging devices and conspiracy between 1989 and 1995.

The company's owner Ronald Kimball, a former Drug Enforcement Administration agent who founded Spy Factory, pleaded guilty to three counts of conspiracy to possess bugging and wire-tapping devices; using false statements to import these devices into the United States and smuggling the devices from Japan.

He faces a possible maximum prison term of 51 to 63 months and fines of $750,000. Kimball also agreed to forfeit about $2.33 million, which represents the proceeds from Spy Factory's sales of thousands of illegal bugging and wiretapping devices between 1989 and 1995.
Marlin Richardson, former general manager, also pleaded guilty to three counts for his role in the scheme and faces a possible maximum prison term of 46 to 57 months and fines of $750,000.
Tracy Ford, former deputy general manager, pleaded guilty to two counts and faces a possible maximum term of six to 12 months and fines of $500,000.
The case had entered its second week of testimony in Manhattan federal court when the defendants agreed to plead guilty.

"We believe that these convictions of the country's largest chain of spy shops and its principals will deal a crushing blow to those who seek to profit on illegal invasions of other people's privacy," White said.
She said that the devices had been purchased by a range of customers that included jealous spouses spying on their husbands and wives.
At the time of the 1995 indictment, the Spy Factory had stores in Arizona, California, Colorado, Georgia, Illinois, Missouri, Nevada, Texas, Utah, and Washington.

The defendants were indicted in August 1995 on charges that they bought devices from the Japanese firm Micro Electronics Ind. Co. of Tokyo, which prosecutors allege is the largest international supplier of illegal bugging and wiretapping devices.
The items included bugging devices that were miniature transmitters hidden in everyday household and office items like pens, calculators and three-plug electric outlet adapters.

Spy Factory also sold so-called "wiretapping devices" that are miniature transmitters which attach directly to telephone lines and are capable of surreptitiously intercepting and transmitting both sides of a telephone conversation to a remote location.
